brief.situation: 14:20 at the nurses' station of a medical unit. You are a staff RN. A well-known local news anchor was admitted this morning to the cardiac unit upstairs. Your colleague and friend Jess, whose own login just locked her out, asks to use yours 'for two minutes' to look at the anchor's chart. She is not on that patient's care team. Work out what is being asked, act on your professional code and the privacy rules, and keep the working relationship where you can.
handover: Your professional code puts the patient first and asks you to protect privacy and confidentiality; you are accountable for your own practice.

Hospital policy: logins are personal and never shared; staff access only the records they need for their job; anyone who learns of a possible privacy breach reports it to the privacy officer the same day.
howItWorks: Choose what to ask or say. Each exchange takes a few minutes of the conversation; Jess answers at once, and the next choice waits for the exchange to finish.
The screen shows Jess, how hard she is pushing, your working relationship, what you know so far, and your note.
When the conversation ends you write your note and explain your reasoning.

reflection.question: For your note: what the privacy problem was, what you did about it and why, and how you dealt with your colleague.

parts.label: The problem
parts.criteria: Names that sharing a login and opening a chart without a job need breach the minimum necessary rule and the code's duty of confidentiality, and that the earlier access is itself a possible breach to report.
parts.modelAnswer: Sharing my login would put her access under my name, and she has no job reason to see that chart. She already looked this morning, which is a possible breach I have to report.

parts.label: Ask, then act
parts.criteria: Finds out whether she is on the care team and what she already did before answering; declines, keeps patient information off phones, and offers the proper route for her own work (the help desk).
parts.modelAnswer: I asked whether she was caring for the patient and whether she'd looked, then said no to my login and the photo and pointed her to the help desk for her own account.

parts.label: The relationship and the channel
parts.criteria: Acknowledges her curiosity without endorsing it; reports to the privacy officer, not by threats or a public post; writes a factual note.
parts.modelAnswer: I stayed kind about it, reported to the privacy officer, and wrote down the facts.

expertPath.text: Ask whether she is on the care team and whether she already looked; acknowledge her curiosity.
Decline your login; point her to the help desk for her own account and her own patients.
Report the earlier access to the privacy officer and write a factual note.

upheld.headline: Privacy kept, colleague kept
upheld.body: You asked before answering, declined kindly, kept patient information off phones, reported the access you learned of, and kept the relationship. That is the expert path.

costly.headline: Kept, at a cost
costly.body: The criteria show the cost: a late answer, a refusal with no way forward, an unreported access, a threat or a public post, or a relationship worse than it needed to be.

breached.headline: Privacy breached
breached.body: A shared login or a photo of patient information is a breach. Curiosity is not a job need; access only what you need for your work.

time_up.headline: Time up
time_up.body: No note was written before the run's limit.

scoring.modelReasoning: Logins are personal and access is limited to what each person needs for their job (the minimum necessary rule; the treatment exception covers the care team, not curiosity). Ask first: Jess is not on the care team and already opened the chart this morning. Acknowledge her curiosity, decline your login and the census-board photo, point her to the help desk for her own work, report the earlier access to the privacy officer as the policy requires, and write a factual note. Avoid threats or public posts.
